    15	
    16	**What it is** — Section 7.2 is Siff's: he states that an overview of his 1989 NSCA presentation and workshop (Siff, 1989) "acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Inference: the five groups below are this entry's grouping, not Siff's; the items inside them are his: movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Quotes from PDF pp. 414-418 are from the text layer.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff's rationale is that "all physical conditioning depends primarily on neuromuscular processes involving sensitive receptors (proprioceptors) in the muscles, tendons and joints," so "Appropriate recruitment of the various stretch reflexes of the body ... forms a vital part of PNF conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Muscle contraction "is really the end-product of the interaction of various voluntary and reflex neuromotor processes," and bodybuilding-style training "over-emphasizes the role of muscle contraction" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). He names the reflexes used: the phasic and tonic components of the myotatic stretch reflex (short and long duration stretching loads give different responses), the Golgi tendon reflex to "reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and reciprocal inhibition, which "can produce a significantly stronger contraction of the agonists" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Maximal contraction through the range ensures "summation," the adding of motor-unit twitches by more units or a higher firing rate (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Use the 23 principles as a checklist when designing or reviewing supplementary exercises: Siff says "employment of any of the above principles in training implies conscious or unconscious reliance on aspects of the PNF system" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Positions as pivots matter in ordinary lifts: a dumbbell curl "with the elbow dug firmly into the side" produces "activation patterns and results which are distinctly different" from one with elbow and shoulder free, and the unrestrained curl adds cheating, trapezius involvement and "downward traction ... at the shoulder joint" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the PNF principles fit best in that small assistance share and in Athletic Medicine handoffs, where multi-joint diagonal patterns can replace single-joint machine work.
    21

    14	# PNF Procedures: Three Activation Techniques, Three Antagonist Reversals and Three Relaxation (Stretching) Techniques
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) lists nine PNF procedures: manual contacts to guide movement; "maximal tolerated resistance"; oral commands and non-verbal cues; maximal stretch reflex in the lengthened range; timing and sequencing; "traction or approximation (compression) to stimulate joint receptors"; "recuperative motion to reduce or avoid fatigue produced by resisted activity"; Specific Activation Techniques; and Specific Relaxation Techniques (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406, text layer). He expands the last two (PDF pp. 417-418 / printed pp. 406-407, text layer):
    17	
    18	- Activation. Repeated Contractions (RC): "precise sequences or patterns of isometric, concentric and eccentric contraction, sometimes augmented by eliciting various neuromuscular reflexes (i.e. methods which may be similar to some types of plyometrics)." Rhythmic Initiation (RI): voluntary relaxation, passive movement and repeated dynamic contractions, "valuable with subjects who struggle to initiate activity because of rigidity or spasticity." Reversal of Antagonists (RA), in three forms: slow reversal (dynamic antagonist contraction, then dynamic agonist contraction); slow reversal-hold (dynamic then isometric contraction of the antagonist, then the same for the agonist); rhythmic stabilisation (isometric antagonist then isometric agonist, "thereby producing co-contraction").
    19	- Relaxation (the techniques coaches call PNF stretching). Contract-Relax (CR): "a dynamic contraction of the antagonist against maximal resistance, followed by a phase of relaxation," repeated from the limit of pain-free range; the practitioner resists "as strongly as possible," tells the client to relax, waits for relaxation, then moves the limb passively "to its new limit of extension" for "a few repetitions." Hold-Relax (HR): the same "except that isometric rather than dynamic contraction against maximal resistance is applied." Slow-Reversal-Hold-Relax (SRHR): "dynamic contraction of the antagonists involved, isometric contraction of the antagonists, brief voluntary relaxation, and finally, dynamic contraction of the agonists," over several repetitions "to enhance functional flexibility."
    20	
    21	**Why it works** — For reversals, Siff's reason is functional: antagonist reversal "occurs naturally in numerous activities such as walking, running and sawing wood," and "If the antagonists do not reverse competently in terms of strength, speed and coordination, motor efficiency is impaired" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For RC: "Repetition of muscle contraction is necessary for motor learning and the development of strength, muscle endurance and flexibility" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For the relaxation techniques the book's reflex rationale is in 7.2.1: prolonged resistance enhances "activation of the Golgi tendon reflex, thereby tending to reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and strong agonist contraction causes reciprocal "reflex relaxation of the antagonist muscles" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404, text layer). Siff does not tie each named technique to a specific reflex. Inference: CR and HR read as uses of the Golgi tendon mechanism and SRHR adds reciprocal inhibition through the final agonist contraction, but that pairing is this entry's reading.
    22	
    23	**When to apply** — Use reversals (slow reversal, rhythmic stabilisation) when the target is coordination between opposing groups, and CR, HR or SRHR when the target is range under control rather than passive range. Siff's 7.5 extension: stretching would gain "markedly" if done "statically and dynamically over a full range with progressively increasing resistance incorporating relevant PNF procedures" instead of "in a static manner separately from the main exercises" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 56, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: warm-ups are where these partner techniques can be observed and dosed daily.
    24	
    25	**When NOT to apply** — These are clinical techniques from Knott and Voss, described here without dosages, rest periods or outcome data; Siff gives none. CR and HR need a partner who can resist "as strongly as possible" and judge relaxation, so they do not scale to large groups without trained staff. Work stays inside "the limit of pain-free action" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), which matches principle 6, "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Rhythmic Initiation is aimed at rigidity or spasticity, a patient problem, not a typical athlete one.
    26	
    27	**Example** — Siff's procedure for CR, as he gives it: move the limb to its pain-free limit, have the client contract the antagonist dynamically while the practitioner resists maximally, command relaxation, wait for it, move the limb passively to its new limit, and repeat "gently for a few repetitions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: for a hamstring, the athlete lies supine with the leg raised to its limit and pushes the heel down against the partner's shoulder, relaxes, and the partner raises the leg further; the book does not name a muscle for this example.

    14	# Novices Should Progress From Mobility to Stability, Following the Developmental Sequences PNF Is Built On
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF methods "were formulated from findings on neuromuscular development, such as the functional evolution of all movement from motor immaturity to motor maturity in the growing child or novice athlete," progressing "total to individuated; proximal to distal, distal to proximal; mobile to stabile; gross to selective; reflexive to deliberate; overlapping to integrative; incoordinate to coordinate" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405, text layer). In 7.2.3.3 he restates the emphasis for "the patient, the novice or the child": "progression from primitive to complex, gross to individuated, mobile to stabile, reflexive to deliberative, proximal to distal, and incoordinate to coordinate." Then: "Contrary to common belief, the novice must be taught from a base of mobility to progress to stability, just as an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff's argument is the developmental analogy itself: the infant moves and staggers before standing stably (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He also states that "all physical conditioning requires a constant interplay of mobility and stability, all patterns implicate some parts of the body in stabilising and other parts in mobilising" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He gives no training study for the novice-athlete claim.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When teaching a beginner a new pattern, let them explore the movement through range before demanding rigid holds, and progress gross to selective and primitive to complex. Principle 21, "Planning of each phase to lay foundations for the next phase," and principle 20, "Progression from primitive to complex actions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), set the order. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the PNF sequence is one way to order those gradual exercise-selection steps for a freshman entering a lifting program.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — This is an analogy from infant motor development extended to novice athletes, with no data in the book: confidence `untested`. The sequences are not one-directional. The 7.2.3 list gives both "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405), the novice paragraph gives "proximal to distal" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407), and principle 18 prescribes "distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Inference: read these as direction by maturity (proximal to distal while immature, distal to proximal once mature), but the book does not say this in one place. Siff names the "common belief" he opposes but does not cite who holds it. For a trained athlete, the goal can be the opposite: "the goal of training may be to prevent motion and to stimulate stability or maintain balance" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Siff's example is developmental, not athletic: "an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). His athletic example of mixed demands: "both static strength and static muscular endurance might have to be developed in the back muscles of an athlete, while three-dimensional dynamic strength, dynamic muscular endurance and dynamic flexibility might have to be developed in the upper leg" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

    14	# Train for a Safety Factor Above Competition Forces, but Strength and Bulk Alone Do Not Protect an Inefficient Athlete
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under "Pattern Deviations and Safety Factors," Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training, so that it is not incorrect to employ patterns of movement which may deviate significantly from those stipulated in PNF" (italics in the original). PNF keeps patterns "close to the body, a situation which occurs seldom in sport," where "forceful or rapid movements have to be executed with the distal extremities far from the relevant joints, thereby imposing large torque on these joints. If training always ensures that this degree of torque or force is avoided, then it will not prepare the athlete for the rigors of the sport and will increase susceptibility to overtraining and injury." Hence: "As in engineering, one must plan for a certain safety factor which allows the athlete to manage even larger forces than those which may be encountered in competition. For example, a safety factor of 1.2 means that a system can cope with a maximal loading of 0.2 or 20% greater than normally expected." Heavy supplementary resistance training ("cross training") serves this, "provided that it does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport." The limit: "Far too many athletes (e.g. in football and rugby) believe that increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury. If one executes a movement in an inefficient manner or reacts too slowly to produce adequate force, then even gigantic strength or structural bulk can be inadequate to prevent injury." (All PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image.)
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff gives the engineering analogy and one sentence of reasoning: "high levels of skill and reactive ability in sport are vital in ensuring that sporting action is efficient and safe" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). No physiological mechanism or data are given. Inference: the claim has two parts, tissue capacity above expected load (the safety factor) and timing and skill to apply it (reactive ability), and the book makes both necessary and neither sufficient.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When an exercise is rejected because it loads a joint at long lever arms, ask whether the sport imposes that torque; if it does, graded exposure is preparation, not risk. When a football player or coach treats added mass as injury armour, use the second half of the passage. Eric's baseline: "Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 140, Inferred (transcript + slides)); and "an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers." (line 141, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: both baseline lines and Siff's passage refuse to equate raw strength with protection.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The 1.2 figure is an engineering illustration, not a measured training target: the book gives no way to measure "forces ... encountered in competition" for a given athlete or joint, and no data that a 20% margin lowers injury. Heavy supplementary work is endorsed only if it "does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Exposure to large torques still has to be progressive; Eric's baseline line 142 treats "abrupt, large changes" as "a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Siff's own: football and rugby players who believe "increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Inference: a lineman whose squat rises 20 kg over an off-season but whose reaction to a cut block is slow is not protected by the squat alone; the book does not give this case.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]] (machines and barbells used for intentional deviation), [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[heuristic--choose-cross-training-by-fitness-qualities-and-phase-not-sport-label]] (5.5, the authors' rules for supplementary "cross training")

15	    14	# PNF Is a Whole Conditioning System Built on Five P-Factors, Not Just a Stretching Method
16	    15	
17	    16	**What it is** — Section 7.2 is Siff's: he states that an overview of his 1989 NSCA presentation and workshop (Siff, 1989) "acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). History: PNF "was developed by Herman Kabat from 1946-1951" on work by Sherrington, Hellebrand, McGraw and Pavlov (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Definition: "a system for promoting the response of neuromuscular mechanisms by stimulating the proprioceptors"; Knott and Voss say its techniques involve "placing a demand where a response is required," which Siff ties to the SAID principle (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Two types: classical PNF, "the hands-on clinical approach described in the Knott and Voss text," and modified PNF, which "adapts certain PNF techniques and principles for application by hand or apparatus in physical conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Inference: the five groups below are this entry's grouping, not Siff's; the items inside them are his: movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Quotes from PDF pp. 414-418 are from the text layer.
18	    17	
19	    18	**Why it works** — Siff's rationale is that "all physical conditioning depends primarily on neuromuscular processes involving sensitive receptors (proprioceptors) in the muscles, tendons and joints," so "Appropriate recruitment of the various stretch reflexes of the body ... forms a vital part of PNF conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Muscle contraction "is really the end-product of the interaction of various voluntary and reflex neuromotor processes," and bodybuilding-style training "over-emphasizes the role of muscle contraction" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). He names the reflexes used: the phasic and tonic components of the myotatic stretch reflex (short and long duration stretching loads give different responses), the Golgi tendon reflex to "reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and reciprocal inhibition, which "can produce a significantly stronger contraction of the agonists" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Maximal contraction through the range ensures "summation," the adding of motor-unit twitches by more units or a higher firing rate (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404).
20	    19	
21	    20	**When to apply** — Use the 23 principles as a checklist when designing or reviewing supplementary exercises: Siff says "employment of any of the above principles in training implies conscious or unconscious reliance on aspects of the PNF system" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). His own scope claim: PNF can improve "all the S-factors of fitness ... except cardiovascular endurance and psychological fitness" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405; see [[framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model]]). Positions as pivots matter in ordinary lifts: a dumbbell curl "with the elbow dug firmly into the side" produces "activation patterns and results which are distinctly different" from one with elbow and shoulder free, and the unrestrained curl adds cheating, trapezius involvement and "downward traction ... at the shoulder joint" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the PNF principles fit best in that small assistance share and in Athletic Medicine handoffs, where multi-joint diagonal patterns can replace single-joint machine work.
22	    21	
23	    22	**When NOT to apply** — Siff's case that PNF is a complete athletic conditioning system is argued, not tested: he gives no training study, and "No training method could be required to offer much more than this repertoire to qualify as an all-round conditioning system" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405) is a judgment. The patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410), so strict PNF is not the goal for athletes (see [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]). Two source oddities: the principles say "Use of distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (principle 18) while the developmental list gives "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405); and procedure 4 attributes the stretch reflex in the lengthened range to "Starling's Law" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: Starling's law is usually stated for cardiac muscle; the book gives no explanation of the link. Classical PNF is hands-on clinical work; Siff points coaches to the NSCA videotapes (Siff, 1989) rather than describing every technique (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
24	    23	
25	    24	**Example** — From 7.5: a coach applying the 7.2 list to a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Figs 7.3-7.8 (PDF pp. 419-420 / printed pp. 408-409, checked against the page images) draw the upper-extremity, lower-extremity and trunk patterns, each labelled with its three component motions (for example "Flexion to Extension, Abduction to Adduction, Ext to Int Rotation").
26	    25	
27	    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-activation-and-relaxation-techniques]], [[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]], [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]], [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]] (the reflexes PNF uses, Fig 3.33), [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (the overflow principle), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (PNF as a stretching category, 3.5.8), [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]] (PNF use of the positive supportive reaction)

42	    14	# PNF Procedures: Three Activation Techniques, Three Antagonist Reversals and Three Relaxation (Stretching) Techniques
43	    15	
44	    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) lists nine PNF procedures: manual contacts to guide movement; "maximal tolerated resistance"; oral commands and non-verbal cues; maximal stretch reflex in the lengthened range; timing and sequencing; "traction or approximation (compression) to stimulate joint receptors"; "recuperative motion to reduce or avoid fatigue produced by resisted activity"; Specific Activation Techniques; and Specific Relaxation Techniques (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406, text layer). He expands the last two (PDF pp. 417-418 / printed pp. 406-407, text layer):
45	    17	
46	    18	- Activation. Repeated Contractions (RC): "precise sequences or patterns of isometric, concentric and eccentric contraction, sometimes augmented by eliciting various neuromuscular reflexes (i.e. methods which may be similar to some types of plyometrics)." Rhythmic Initiation (RI): voluntary relaxation, passive movement and repeated dynamic contractions, "valuable with subjects who struggle to initiate activity because of rigidity or spasticity." Reversal of Antagonists (RA), in three forms: slow reversal (dynamic antagonist contraction, then dynamic agonist contraction); slow reversal-hold (dynamic then isometric contraction of the antagonist, then the same for the agonist); rhythmic stabilisation (isometric antagonist then isometric agonist, "thereby producing co-contraction").
47	    19	- Relaxation (the techniques coaches call PNF stretching). Contract-Relax (CR): "a dynamic contraction of the antagonist against maximal resistance, followed by a phase of relaxation," repeated from the limit of pain-free range; the practitioner resists "as strongly as possible," tells the client to relax, waits for relaxation, then moves the limb passively "to its new limit of extension" for "a few repetitions." Hold-Relax (HR): the same "except that isometric rather than dynamic contraction against maximal resistance is applied." Slow-Reversal-Hold-Relax (SRHR): "dynamic contraction of the antagonists involved, isometric contraction of the antagonists, brief voluntary relaxation, and finally, dynamic contraction of the agonists," over several repetitions "to enhance functional flexibility."
48	    20	
49	    21	**Why it works** — For reversals, Siff's reason is functional: antagonist reversal "occurs naturally in numerous activities such as walking, running and sawing wood," and "If the antagonists do not reverse competently in terms of strength, speed and coordination, motor efficiency is impaired" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For RC: "Repetition of muscle contraction is necessary for motor learning and the development of strength, muscle endurance and flexibility" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For the relaxation techniques the book's reflex rationale is in 7.2.1: prolonged resistance enhances "activation of the Golgi tendon reflex, thereby tending to reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and strong agonist contraction causes reciprocal "reflex relaxation of the antagonist muscles" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404, text layer). Siff does not tie each named technique to a specific reflex. Inference: CR and HR read as uses of the Golgi tendon mechanism and SRHR adds reciprocal inhibition through the final agonist contraction, but that pairing is this entry's reading.
50	    22	
51	    23	**When to apply** — Use reversals (slow reversal, rhythmic stabilisation) when the target is coordination between opposing groups, and CR, HR or SRHR when the target is range under control rather than passive range. Siff's 7.5 extension: stretching would gain "markedly" if done "statically and dynamically over a full range with progressively increasing resistance incorporating relevant PNF procedures" instead of "in a static manner separately from the main exercises" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 56, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: warm-ups are where these partner techniques can be observed and dosed daily.
52	    24	
53	    25	**When NOT to apply** — These are clinical techniques from Knott and Voss, described here without dosages, rest periods or outcome data; Siff gives none. CR and HR need a partner who can resist "as strongly as possible" and judge relaxation, so they do not scale to large groups without trained staff. Work stays inside "the limit of pain-free action" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), which matches principle 6, "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Rhythmic Initiation is aimed at rigidity or spasticity, a patient problem, not a typical athlete one.
54	    26	
55	    27	**Example** — Siff's procedure for CR, as he gives it: move the limb to its pain-free limit, have the client contract the antagonist dynamically while the practitioner resists maximally, command relaxation, wait for it, move the limb passively to its new limit, and repeat "gently for a few repetitions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: for a hamstring, the athlete lies supine with the leg raised to its limit and pushes the heel down against the partner's shoulder, relaxes, and the partner raises the leg further; the book does not name a muscle for this example.
56	    28	
57	    29	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]], [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]] (CR and HR as relaxation methods, 3.5.9), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (where PNF stretching sits among stretching types), [[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]

72	    14	# Novices Should Progress From Mobility to Stability, Following the Developmental Sequences PNF Is Built On
73	    15	
74	    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF methods "were formulated from findings on neuromuscular development, such as the functional evolution of all movement from motor immaturity to motor maturity in the growing child or novice athlete," progressing "total to individuated; proximal to distal, distal to proximal; mobile to stabile; gross to selective; reflexive to deliberate; overlapping to integrative; incoordinate to coordinate" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405, text layer). In 7.2.3.3 he restates the emphasis for "the patient, the novice or the child": "progression from primitive to complex, gross to individuated, mobile to stabile, reflexive to deliberative, proximal to distal, and incoordinate to coordinate." Then: "Contrary to common belief, the novice must be taught from a base of mobility to progress to stability, just as an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer).
75	    17	
76	    18	**Why it works** — Siff's argument is the developmental analogy itself: the infant moves and staggers before standing stably (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He also states that "all physical conditioning requires a constant interplay of mobility and stability, all patterns implicate some parts of the body in stabilising and other parts in mobilising" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He gives no training study for the novice-athlete claim.
77	    19	
78	    20	**When to apply** — When teaching a beginner a new pattern, let them explore the movement through range before demanding rigid holds, and progress gross to selective and primitive to complex. Principle 21, "Planning of each phase to lay foundations for the next phase," and principle 20, "Progression from primitive to complex actions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), set the order. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the PNF sequence is one way to order those gradual exercise-selection steps for a freshman entering a lifting program.
79	    21	
80	    22	**When NOT to apply** — This is an analogy from infant motor development extended to novice athletes, with no data in the book: confidence `untested`. The sequences are not one-directional. The 7.2.3 list gives both "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405), the novice paragraph gives "proximal to distal" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407), and principle 18 prescribes "distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Inference: read these as direction by maturity (proximal to distal while immature, distal to proximal once mature), but the book does not say this in one place. Siff names the "common belief" he opposes but does not cite who holds it. For a trained athlete, the goal can be the opposite: "the goal of training may be to prevent motion and to stimulate stability or maintain balance" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
81	    23	
82	    24	**Example** — Siff's example is developmental, not athletic: "an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). His athletic example of mixed demands: "both static strength and static muscular endurance might have to be developed in the back muscles of an athlete, while three-dimensional dynamic strength, dynamic muscular endurance and dynamic flexibility might have to be developed in the upper leg" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
83	    25	
84	    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]] (moved and stabilised joints, 3.7), [[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]

PNF keeps patterns "close to the body, a situation which occurs seldom in sport," where "forceful or rapid movements have to be executed with the distal extremities far from the relevant joints, thereby imposing large torque on these joints. If training always ensures that this degree of torque or force is avoided, then it will not prepare the athlete for the rigors of the sport and will increase susceptibility to overtraining and injury." Hence: "As in engineering, one must plan for a certain safety factor which allows the athlete to manage even larger forces than those which may be encountered in competition. For example, a safety factor of 1.2 means that a system can cope with a maximal loading of 0.2 or 20% greater than normally expected." Heavy supplementary resistance training ("cross training") serves this, "provided that it does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport." The limit: "Far too many athletes (e.g. in football and rugby) believe that increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury. If one executes a movement in an inefficient manner or reacts too slowly to produce adequate force, then even gigantic strength or structural bulk can be inadequate to prevent injury." (All PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image.)
129	    17	
130	    18	**Why it works** — Siff gives the engineering analogy and one sentence of reasoning: "high levels of skill and reactive ability in sport are vital in ensuring that sporting action is efficient and safe" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). No physiological mechanism or data are given. Inference: the claim has two parts, tissue capacity above expected load (the safety factor) and timing and skill to apply it (reactive ability), and the book makes both necessary and neither sufficient.
131	    19	
132	    20	**When to apply** — When an exercise is rejected because it loads a joint at long lever arms, ask whether the sport imposes that torque; if it does, graded exposure is preparation, not risk. When a football player or coach treats added mass as injury armour, use the second half of the passage. Eric's baseline: "Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 140, Inferred (transcript + slides)); and "an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers." (line 141, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: both baseline lines and Siff's passage refuse to equate raw strength with protection.
133	    21	
134	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The 1.2 figure is an engineering illustration, not a measured training target: the book gives no way to measure "forces ... encountered in competition" for a given athlete or joint, and no data that a 20% margin lowers injury. Heavy supplementary work is endorsed only if it "does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Exposure to large torques still has to be progressive; Eric's baseline line 142 treats "abrupt, large changes" as "a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)).
135	    23	
136	    24	**Example** — Siff's own: football and rugby players who believe "increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Inference: a lineman whose squat rises 20 kg over an off-season but whose reaction to a cut block is slow is not protected by the squat alone; the book does not give this case.
137	    25	
138	    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]] (machines and barbells used for intentional deviation), [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[heuristic--choose-cross-training-by-fitness-qualities-and-phase-not-sport-label]] (5.5, the authors' rules for supplementary "cross training")

153	    14	# "Functional Training" Is Only a Synonym for Sport-Specific Training, and No Single Exercise Is "Non-Functional"
154	    15	
155	    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) proposes replacing "modified PNF" with Functional Neuromuscular Conditioning (FNC), for five reasons: it is "sometimes desirable to deviate from strict PNF principles"; other disciplines ("Feldenkrais, Alexander, yoga, Tai Chi and Laban") add methods; contraction "may be facilitated by local after-discharge of the same muscle," so not all is neuromuscular; some PNF methods "may not be classified accurately as proprioceptive, such as cognitive, perceptual and other sensory mechanisms"; and the full name "is too technically daunting for the average coach or athlete." FNC "should be regarded as an entire conditioning system capable of developing any desired type of musculoskeletal fitness." He then turns to the fashion term: "Lately, the term 'functional training' has been promoted as a unique and modern method of training. In fact, it is nothing much more than a synonym for 'action specific', 'activity specific' or 'sport specific' training." To be accurate it "should address not only the motor qualities, but also the metabolic requirements of a given activity." And: "it is misleading to classify a single exercise as being "non-functional", since functional conditioning can comprise a combination of general and specific, 'functional' and 'non-functional' exercises. Indeed, this type of combined GPP and SPP methods forms the basis of all periodisation." (All PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image.)
156	    17	
157	    18	**Why it works** — The argument is from programme level, not exercise level: function is a property of the whole combination of general (GPP) and specific (SPP) means over time, so labelling one exercise cannot settle it (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). Siff adds that "Because Wolff's Law states that function precedes structure, FNC may be seen to embrace all-round development of function and structure" (same page). Inference: Wolff's law is usually stated for bone remodelling under load; the book extends it here without further explanation.
158	    19	
159	    20	**When to apply** — When a coach, vendor or athlete calls an exercise "functional" or "non-functional," ask which motor and metabolic demands of the sport it serves and where it sits in the GPP-to-SPP sequence. Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: Siff's point and the baseline agree; both replace a yes-or-no "functional" label with a position on a general-to-specific spectrum.
160	    21	
161	    22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology argument with no data, so `untested`. It does not mean every exercise transfers equally: elsewhere the book sets strict criteria for transfer ([[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]]) and warns that inappropriate resistance patterns "can be detrimental to the performance of the actual sporting movements" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). "Functional" here differs from the Chapter 1 sense of "functional" versus "structural" training ([[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]]), which is about neural versus hypertrophic effects, so check which meaning a source uses.
162	    23	
163	    24	**Example** — Inference: a back squat is "non-functional" for a wide receiver only if judged alone; as a GPP means early in the off-season, followed by more specific acceleration and jump work, it is part of a functional programme in Siff's sense. The book gives no worked example for this section.
164	    25	
165	    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (a different use of "functional"), [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]], [[claim--core-stability-balance-training-has-no-shown-transfer-to-sport]] (7.4, the book's objection to another "functional" fashion)

180	    14	# Fradd (1995): Elbow Flexion Under Free Weight, Isokinetic and Combined Resistance
181	    15	
182	    16	**What it is** — The authors report a study in which "the same group of subjects" did elbow flexion under free-weight (isoinertial), isokinetic, and combined resistance, the combination applied "using a cable machine specially designed and constructed for this purpose by one of Siff's mechanical engineering students at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa (Fradd, 1995)" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412, checked against the page image). Number of subjects, their training status, loads and isokinetic speed are not given. Table 7.1 (velocity in m/s, power in W, force in N):
183	    17	
184	    18	| Resistance | Max velocity | Mean power | Peak power | Mean force | Peak force |
185	    19	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
186	    20	| Isoinertial | 1.49 | 151 | 306 | 184 | 219 |
187	    21	| Isokinetic | 0.42 | 80 | 129 | 247 | 350 |
188	    22	| Combined | 0.38 | 102 | 131 | 336 | 380 |
189	    23	
190	    24	The five stated findings: (1) "Greatest mean and peak power is produced under free weight conditions, reaching a peak approximately midway through the movement"; (2) "Free weight force production is greatest during the earliest phases of joint movement"; (3) isokinetic and combined power is "considerably lower" but "remains near its peak value for a considerable part of the range"; (4) "Mean and peak force production is greatest during combined conditions, and may peak twice during the movement, most commonly near the beginning and the end of range"; (5) "Isokinetic force plateaus about one-third through the range, but commonly increases near end of range" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412). For Fig 7.10 the text adds that peak power and velocity come "about halfway through the movement, when elbow angle is approximately 90 degrees," that "Approximately half the movement is spent in acceleration and half in deceleration," and that free-weight peak power is "some three times greater than under isokinetic or combined auxotonic-isokinetic conditions" (PDF p. 424 / printed p. 413, checked against the page image).
191	    25	
192	    26	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the differences beyond the resistance types themselves. They stress variability: curve shape "varies with every individual, according to their motor characteristics, and, in the combined scenario, with the magnitude of the inertial load and the velocity of isokinetic resistance"; combined resistance "may be made more auxotonic (free weight) if the added weight is large and more isokinetic if the added load is relatively small" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412). Inference: free weight lets the load accelerate and then forces deceleration, which yields high peak power mid-range; an isokinetic device caps velocity, so force can stay high while power stays low.
193	    27	
194	    28	**When to apply** — When choosing a resistance mode for a goal: free weight for peak power, combined resistance for high force across the range. The authors' rule for all variable resistance: "it is important to fully understand the emphasis of the resistance training being used, because frequent use of any inappropriate training method or resistance pattern can be detrimental to the performance of the actual sporting movements," and for maximal power, "train regularly with loads that do not exceed about 60-70 percent of one's maximum" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides)).
195	    29	
196	    30	**When NOT to apply** — One single-joint movement, one unreported sample, a student project: confidence `untested`. Four places where the section does not line up with itself, (a) to (c) read from the page images and (d) text against data: (a) Table 7.1 gives 306 W against 129 and 131 W, about 2.4 times, while the text says "some three times greater" (PDF pp. 423-424). Inference: Figs 7.10-7.12 show peak power of about 350 against about 125-130 on the plotted scale, nearer three times, so the text may describe the figures rather than the table. (b) Fig 7.10's force curve starts at about 170 and peaks at about 230 near 20-40% of displacement, then declines slowly; the text says peak force is "near the beginning" (PDF p. 424). (c) Fig 7.12's combined force curve rises to about 350 by about 30%, holds, and is highest at about 85-90% before a sharp drop at the end; the double peak "near the beginning and the end of range" in finding 4 is not visible in this printed curve (PDF p. 424). (d) The 7.3 opening says greatest force is "usually ... possible after the joint has passed through the midpoint of the movement" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411), yet the free-weight data here put force highest early. Inference: the opening speaks of maximal joint strength across the range; Fig 7.10 shows force applied to a given accelerating load. Zatsiorsky describes ascending, descending and concave strength curves, with elbow flexion strongest at about 90 degrees ([[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]]), so "after the midpoint" is not a general rule. Velocity and acceleration in Figs 7.10-7.12 share one unlabelled axis with force and power, so their plotted heights cannot be read as m/s.
197	    31	
198	    32	**Example** — The study itself: in the combined condition, mean force was 336 N against 184 N under free weight, while peak power was 131 W against 306 W (Table 7.1, PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412, checked against the page image).
199	    33	
200	    34	**Related** — [[case-study--box-squat-with-free-weights-plus-elastic-bands]] (the second hybrid in 7.3), [[framework--isokinetic-method-claimed-advantages-and-mechanism]] (4.2.6.1), [[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (the authors' free-weight alternative, named in the 7.3 opening), [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]], [[research-papers/frost-2010-a-biomechanical-evaluation-of-resistance]] (mechanics of constant, isokinetic and variable resistance)

    14	# PNF Is a Whole Conditioning System Built on Five P-Factors, Not Just a Stretching Method
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Section 7.2 is Siff's: he states that an overview of his 1989 NSCA presentation and workshop (Siff, 1989) "acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). History: PNF "was developed by Herman Kabat from 1946-1951" on work by Sherrington, Hellebrand, McGraw and Pavlov (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Definition: "a system for promoting the response of neuromuscular mechanisms by stimulating the proprioceptors"; Knott and Voss say its techniques involve "placing a demand where a response is required," which Siff ties to the SAID principle (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Two types: classical PNF, "the hands-on clinical approach described in the Knott and Voss text," and modified PNF, which "adapts certain PNF techniques and principles for application by hand or apparatus in physical conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Inference: the five groups below are this entry's grouping, not Siff's; the items inside them are his: movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Quotes from PDF pp. 414-418 are from the text layer.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff's rationale is that "all physical conditioning depends primarily on neuromuscular processes involving sensitive receptors (proprioceptors) in the muscles, tendons and joints," so "Appropriate recruitment of the various stretch reflexes of the body ... forms a vital part of PNF conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Muscle contraction "is really the end-product of the interaction of various voluntary and reflex neuromotor processes," and bodybuilding-style training "over-emphasizes the role of muscle contraction" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). He names the reflexes used: the phasic and tonic components of the myotatic stretch reflex (short and long duration stretching loads give different responses), the Golgi tendon reflex to "reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and reciprocal inhibition, which "can produce a significantly stronger contraction of the agonists" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Maximal contraction through the range ensures "summation," the adding of motor-unit twitches by more units or a higher firing rate (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Use the 23 principles as a checklist when designing or reviewing supplementary exercises: Siff says "employment of any of the above principles in training implies conscious or unconscious reliance on aspects of the PNF system" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). His own scope claim: PNF can improve "all the S-factors of fitness ... except cardiovascular endurance and psychological fitness" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405; see [[framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model]]). Positions as pivots matter in ordinary lifts: a dumbbell curl "with the elbow dug firmly into the side" produces "activation patterns and results which are distinctly different" from one with elbow and shoulder free, and the unrestrained curl adds cheating, trapezius involvement and "downward traction ... at the shoulder joint" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the PNF principles fit best in that small assistance share and in Athletic Medicine handoffs, where multi-joint diagonal patterns can replace single-joint machine work.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Siff's case that PNF is a complete athletic conditioning system is argued, not tested: he gives no training study, and "No training method could be required to offer much more than this repertoire to qualify as an all-round conditioning system" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405) is a judgment. The patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410), so strict PNF is not the goal for athletes (see [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]). Two source oddities: the principles say "Use of distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (principle 18) while the developmental list gives "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405); and procedure 4 attributes the stretch reflex in the lengthened range to "Starling's Law" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: Starling's law is usually stated for cardiac muscle; the book gives no explanation of the link. Classical PNF is hands-on clinical work; Siff points coaches to the NSCA videotapes (Siff, 1989) rather than describing every technique (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
    23	
    24	**Example** — From 7.5: a coach applying the 7.2 list to a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Figs 7.3-7.8 (PDF pp. 419-420 / printed pp. 408-409, checked against the page images) draw the upper-extremity, lower-extremity and trunk patterns, each labelled with its three component motions (for example "Flexion to Extension, Abduction to Adduction, Ext to Int Rotation").
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-activation-and-relaxation-techniques]], [[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]], [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]], [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]] (the reflexes PNF uses, Fig 3.33), [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (the overflow principle), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (PNF as a stretching category, 3.5.8), [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]] (PNF use of the positive supportive reaction)

    13	
    14	# PNF Procedures: Three Activation Techniques, Three Antagonist Reversals and Three Relaxation (Stretching) Techniques
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) lists nine PNF procedures: manual contacts to guide movement; "maximal tolerated resistance"; oral commands and non-verbal cues; maximal stretch reflex in the lengthened range; timing and sequencing; "traction or approximation (compression) to stimulate joint receptors"; "recuperative motion to reduce or avoid fatigue produced by resisted activity"; Specific Activation Techniques; and Specific Relaxation Techniques (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406, text layer). He expands the last two (PDF pp. 417-418 / printed pp. 406-407, text layer):
    17	
    18	- Activation. Repeated Contractions (RC): "precise sequences or patterns of isometric, concentric and eccentric contraction, sometimes augmented by eliciting various neuromuscular reflexes (i.e. methods which may be similar to some types of plyometrics)." Rhythmic Initiation (RI): voluntary relaxation, passive movement and repeated dynamic contractions, "valuable with subjects who struggle to initiate activity because of rigidity or spasticity." Reversal of Antagonists (RA), in three forms: slow reversal (dynamic antagonist contraction, then dynamic agonist contraction); slow reversal-hold (dynamic then isometric contraction of the antagonist, then the same for the agonist); rhythmic stabilisation (isometric antagonist then isometric agonist, "thereby producing co-contraction").
    19	- Relaxation (the techniques coaches call PNF stretching). Contract-Relax (CR): "a dynamic contraction of the antagonist against maximal resistance, followed by a phase of relaxation," repeated from the limit of pain-free range; the practitioner resists "as strongly as possible," tells the client to relax, waits for relaxation, then moves the limb passively "to its new limit of extension" for "a few repetitions." Hold-Relax (HR): the same "except that isometric rather than dynamic contraction against maximal resistance is applied." Slow-Reversal-Hold-Relax (SRHR): "dynamic contraction of the antagonists involved, isometric contraction of the antagonists, brief voluntary relaxation, and finally, dynamic contraction of the agonists," over several repetitions "to enhance functional flexibility."
    20	
    21	**Why it works** — For reversals, Siff's reason is functional: antagonist reversal "occurs naturally in numerous activities such as walking, running and sawing wood," and "If the antagonists do not reverse competently in terms of strength, speed and coordination, motor efficiency is impaired" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For RC: "Repetition of muscle contraction is necessary for motor learning and the development of strength, muscle endurance and flexibility" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For the relaxation techniques the book's reflex rationale is in 7.2.1: prolonged resistance enhances "activation of the Golgi tendon reflex, thereby tending to reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and strong agonist contraction causes reciprocal "reflex relaxation of the antagonist muscles" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404, text layer). Siff does not tie each named technique to a specific reflex. Inference: CR and HR read as uses of the Golgi tendon mechanism and SRHR adds reciprocal inhibition through the final agonist contraction, but that pairing is this entry's reading.
    22	
    23	**When to apply** — Use reversals (slow reversal, rhythmic stabilisation) when the target is coordination between opposing groups, and CR, HR or SRHR when the target is range under control rather than passive range. Siff's 7.5 extension: stretching would gain "markedly" if done "statically and dynamically over a full range with progressively increasing resistance incorporating relevant PNF procedures" instead of "in a static manner separately from the main exercises" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 56, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: warm-ups are where these partner techniques can be observed and dosed daily.
    24	
    25	**When NOT to apply** — These are clinical techniques from Knott and Voss, described here without dosages, rest periods or outcome data; Siff gives none. CR and HR need a partner who can resist "as strongly as possible" and judge relaxation, so they do not scale to large groups without trained staff. Work stays inside "the limit of pain-free action" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), which matches principle 6, "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Rhythmic Initiation is aimed at rigidity or spasticity, a patient problem, not a typical athlete one.
    26	
    27	**Example** — Siff's procedure for CR, as he gives it: move the limb to its pain-free limit, have the client contract the antagonist dynamically while the practitioner resists maximally, command relaxation, wait for it, move the limb passively to its new limit, and repeat "gently for a few repetitions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: for a hamstring, the athlete lies supine with the leg raised to its limit and pushes the heel down against the partner's shoulder, relaxes, and the partner raises the leg further; the book does not name a muscle for this example.
    28	
    29	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]], [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]] (CR and HR as relaxation methods, 3.5.9), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (where PNF stretching sits among stretching types), [[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]

    14	# Novices Should Progress From Mobility to Stability, Following the Developmental Sequences PNF Is Built On
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF methods "were formulated from findings on neuromuscular development, such as the functional evolution of all movement from motor immaturity to motor maturity in the growing child or novice athlete," progressing "total to individuated; proximal to distal, distal to proximal; mobile to stabile; gross to selective; reflexive to deliberate; overlapping to integrative; incoordinate to coordinate" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405, text layer). In 7.2.3.3 he restates the emphasis for "the patient, the novice or the child": "progression from primitive to complex, gross to individuated, mobile to stabile, reflexive to deliberative, proximal to distal, and incoordinate to coordinate." Then: "Contrary to common belief, the novice must be taught from a base of mobility to progress to stability, just as an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff's argument is the developmental analogy itself: the infant moves and staggers before standing stably (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He also states that "all physical conditioning requires a constant interplay of mobility and stability, all patterns implicate some parts of the body in stabilising and other parts in mobilising" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He gives no training study for the novice-athlete claim.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When teaching a beginner a new pattern, let them explore the movement through range before demanding rigid holds, and progress gross to selective and primitive to complex. Principle 21, "Planning of each phase to lay foundations for the next phase," and principle 20, "Progression from primitive to complex actions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), set the order. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the PNF sequence is one way to order those gradual exercise-selection steps for a freshman entering a lifting program.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — This is an analogy from infant motor development extended to novice athletes, with no data in the book: confidence `untested`. The sequences are not one-directional. The 7.2.3 list gives both "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405), the novice paragraph gives "proximal to distal" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407), and principle 18 prescribes "distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Inference: read these as direction by maturity (proximal to distal while immature, distal to proximal once mature), but the book does not say this in one place. Siff names the "common belief" he opposes but does not cite who holds it. For a trained athlete, the goal can be the opposite: "the goal of training may be to prevent motion and to stimulate stability or maintain balance" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Siff's example is developmental, not athletic: "an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). His athletic example of mixed demands: "both static strength and static muscular endurance might have to be developed in the back muscles of an athlete, while three-dimensional dynamic strength, dynamic muscular endurance and dynamic flexibility might have to be developed in the upper leg" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]] (moved and stabilised joints, 3.7), [[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]

    14	# Rank Equipment by How Well It Allows Spiral-Diagonal Patterns: Pulleys and Dumbbells First, Barbells Next, Machines Last
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) ranks equipment for modified PNF: "Pulleys and dumbbells are especially suitable for application of the spiral and diagonal, midline-crossing PNF techniques. ... Barbell training provides fewer opportunities for the use of PNF training, while machines offer the fewest possibilities of all" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Patterns are "Probably the most neglected aspect of PNF by coaches" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer). "No machines other than the traditional high-low pulley machines allow the user to produce PNF patterns," and "pec-decks, back hyperextension machines, seated pressing machines, hack-squat machines and leg extension machines ... cause such large deviations from recommended PNF patterns that they can impose excessive loading on certain joints and are suitable only for a small proportion of the training of highly conditioned athletes" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer). Machine training "requires a disproportionate number of machines to approximate the training offered by free weight and pulley training in three-dimensional space" (same page).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff's reason is pattern fidelity: PNF patterns "stimulate more thorough involvement and motor development than the less-than-optimal patterns imposed by the abundance of linear or cam machines" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). Machine design "imposes body positions, postures and activation of pivots which usually differ considerably from those recommended by PNF and compromise the effectiveness and safety of the exercise" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). He calls the belief that machines offer "greater stability and safety for beginners than free weights" "A major error," and concludes "instructors must always 'spot' for the users of machines as well as free weights" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When choosing assistance exercises for rotational or overhead athletes, prefer cable and dumbbell versions that let the limb cross the midline and rotate. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: this heuristic applies inside that small assistance share; it does not argue for replacing the barbell core lifts.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Siff says it "does not imply that barbell and machine training should be avoided": they "can be used effectively under special circumstances, sometimes to cause intentional deviations from PNF patterns to adapt the body to potentially harmful actions which may occur in real sporting situations" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). No comparative data are given for the ranking or for the joint-loading claims about named machines. The "excessive loading" judgment on pec-decks and leg extensions is Siff's opinion in this passage. Inference: in rehab settings where Athletic Medicine wants a fixed path, a machine's constraint can be the point.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Siff's examples: "The standing full-range cable cross-over exercise with external-internal rotation of the shoulder joint furnishes just one example of an adapted PNF pattern" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410); and in 7.5, for a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, cable-crossovers "in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern ... that cross the sagittal midline of the body" instead of the pec-deck (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Fig 7.8's caption adds that the trunk rotation pattern can be done supine or standing and "Resistance may be offered with a cable machine" (PDF p. 420 / printed p. 409, checked against the page image).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]] (4.2.7.1), [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] (4.2.7, the same "not safer than free weights" point), [[heuristic--equip-circuits-with-free-weights-and-pulleys-over-multistation-machines]], [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]

    13	
    14	# Train for a Safety Factor Above Competition Forces, but Strength and Bulk Alone Do Not Protect an Inefficient Athlete
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under "Pattern Deviations and Safety Factors," Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training, so that it is not incorrect to employ patterns of movement which may deviate significantly from those stipulated in PNF" (italics in the original). PNF keeps patterns "close to the body, a situation which occurs seldom in sport," where "forceful or rapid movements have to be executed with the distal extremities far from the relevant joints, thereby imposing large torque on these joints. If training always ensures that this degree of torque or force is avoided, then it will not prepare the athlete for the rigors of the sport and will increase susceptibility to overtraining and injury." Hence: "As in engineering, one must plan for a certain safety factor which allows the athlete to manage even larger forces than those which may be encountered in competition. For example, a safety factor of 1.2 means that a system can cope with a maximal loading of 0.2 or 20% greater than normally expected." Heavy supplementary resistance training ("cross training") serves this, "provided that it does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport." The limit: "Far too many athletes (e.g. in football and rugby) believe that increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury. If one executes a movement in an inefficient manner or reacts too slowly to produce adequate force, then even gigantic strength or structural bulk can be inadequate to prevent injury." (All PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image.)
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Siff gives the engineering analogy and one sentence of reasoning: "high levels of skill and reactive ability in sport are vital in ensuring that sporting action is efficient and safe" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). No physiological mechanism or data are given. Inference: the claim has two parts, tissue capacity above expected load (the safety factor) and timing and skill to apply it (reactive ability), and the book makes both necessary and neither sufficient.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When an exercise is rejected because it loads a joint at long lever arms, ask whether the sport imposes that torque; if it does, graded exposure is preparation, not risk. When a football player or coach treats added mass as injury armour, use the second half of the passage. Eric's baseline: "Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 140, Inferred (transcript + slides)); and "an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers." (line 141, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: both baseline lines and Siff's passage refuse to equate raw strength with protection.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The 1.2 figure is an engineering illustration, not a measured training target: the book gives no way to measure "forces ... encountered in competition" for a given athlete or joint, and no data that a 20% margin lowers injury. Heavy supplementary work is endorsed only if it "does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Exposure to large torques still has to be progressive; Eric's baseline line 142 treats "abrupt, large changes" as "a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Siff's own: football and rugby players who believe "increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Inference: a lineman whose squat rises 20 kg over an off-season but whose reaction to a cut block is slow is not protected by the squat alone; the book does not give this case.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]] (machines and barbells used for intentional deviation), [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[heuristic--choose-cross-training-by-fitness-qualities-and-phase-not-sport-label]] (5.5, the authors' rules for supplementary "cross training")
