    13	
    14	# "Functional Training" Is Only a Synonym for Sport-Specific Training, and No Single Exercise Is "Non-Functional"
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) proposes replacing "modified PNF" with Functional Neuromuscular Conditioning (FNC), for five reasons: it is "sometimes desirable to deviate from strict PNF principles"; other disciplines ("Feldenkrais, Alexander, yoga, Tai Chi and Laban") add methods; contraction "may be facilitated by local after-discharge of the same muscle," so not all is neuromuscular; some PNF methods "may not be classified accurately as proprioceptive, such as cognitive, perceptual and other sensory mechanisms"; and the full name "is too technically daunting for the average coach or athlete." FNC "should be regarded as an entire conditioning system capable of developing any desired type of musculoskeletal fitness." He then turns to the fashion term: "Lately, the term 'functional training' has been promoted as a unique and modern method of training. In fact, it is nothing much more than a synonym for 'action specific', 'activity specific' or 'sport specific' training." To be accurate it "should address not only the motor qualities, but also the metabolic requirements of a given activity." And: "it is misleading to classify a single exercise as being "non-functional", since functional conditioning can comprise a combination of general and specific, 'functional' and 'non-functional' exercises. Indeed, this type of combined GPP and SPP methods forms the basis of all periodisation." (All PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image.)
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The argument is from programme level, not exercise level: function is a property of the whole combination of general (GPP) and specific (SPP) means over time, so labelling one exercise cannot settle it (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). Siff adds that "Because Wolff's Law states that function precedes structure, FNC may be seen to embrace all-round development of function and structure" (same page). Inference: Wolff's law is usually stated for bone remodelling under load; the book extends it here without further explanation.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a coach, vendor or athlete calls an exercise "functional" or "non-functional," ask which motor and metabolic demands of the sport it serves and where it sits in the GPP-to-SPP sequence. Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: Siff's point and the baseline agree; both replace a yes-or-no "functional" label with a position on a general-to-specific spectrum.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology argument with no data, so `untested`. It does not mean every exercise transfers equally: elsewhere the book sets strict criteria for transfer ([[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]]) and warns that inappropriate resistance patterns "can be detrimental to the performance of the actual sporting movements" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). "Functional" here differs from the Chapter 1 sense of "functional" versus "structural" training ([[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]]), which is about neural versus hypertrophic effects, so check which meaning a source uses.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Inference: a back squat is "non-functional" for a wide receiver only if judged alone; as a GPP means early in the off-season, followed by more specific acceleration and jump work, it is part of a functional programme in Siff's sense. The book gives no worked example for this section.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (a different use of "functional"), [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]], [[claim--core-stability-balance-training-has-no-shown-transfer-to-sport]] (7.4, the book's objection to another "functional" fashion)

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Fradd (1995): Elbow Flexion Under Free Weight, Isokinetic and Combined Resistance
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors report a study in which "the same group of subjects" did elbow flexion under free-weight (isoinertial), isokinetic, and combined resistance, the combination applied "using a cable machine specially designed and constructed for this purpose by one of Siff's mechanical engineering students at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa (Fradd, 1995)" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412, checked against the page image). Number of subjects, their training status, loads and isokinetic speed are not given. Table 7.1 (velocity in m/s, power in W, force in N):
    17	
    18	| Resistance | Max velocity | Mean power | Peak power | Mean force | Peak force |
    19	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    20	| Isoinertial | 1.49 | 151 | 306 | 184 | 219 |
    21	| Isokinetic | 0.42 | 80 | 129 | 247 | 350 |
    22	| Combined | 0.38 | 102 | 131 | 336 | 380 |
    23	
    24	The five stated findings: (1) "Greatest mean and peak power is produced under free weight conditions, reaching a peak approximately midway through the movement"; (2) "Free weight force production is greatest during the earliest phases of joint movement"; (3) isokinetic and combined power is "considerably lower" but "remains near its peak value for a considerable part of the range"; (4) "Mean and peak force production is greatest during combined conditions, and may peak twice during the movement, most commonly near the beginning and the end of range"; (5) "Isokinetic force plateaus about one-third through the range, but commonly increases near end of range" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412). For Fig 7.10 the text adds that peak power and velocity come "about halfway through the movement, when elbow angle is approximately 90 degrees," that "Approximately half the movement is spent in acceleration and half in deceleration," and that free-weight peak power is "some three times greater than under isokinetic or combined auxotonic-isokinetic conditions" (PDF p. 424 / printed p. 413, checked against the page image).
    25	
    26	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the differences beyond the resistance types themselves. They stress variability: curve shape "varies with every individual, according to their motor characteristics, and, in the combined scenario, with the magnitude of the inertial load and the velocity of isokinetic resistance"; combined resistance "may be made more auxotonic (free weight) if the added weight is large and more isokinetic if the added load is relatively small" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412). Inference: free weight lets the load accelerate and then forces deceleration, which yields high peak power mid-range; an isokinetic device caps velocity, so force can stay high while power stays low.
    27	
    28	**When to apply** — When choosing a resistance mode for a goal: free weight for peak power, combined resistance for high force across the range. The authors' rule for all variable resistance: "it is important to fully understand the emphasis of the resistance training being used, because frequent use of any inappropriate training method or resistance pattern can be detrimental to the performance of the actual sporting movements," and for maximal power, "train regularly with loads that do not exceed about 60-70 percent of one's maximum" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides)).
    29	
    30	**When NOT to apply** — One single-joint movement, one unreported sample, a student project: confidence `untested`. Four places where the section does not line up with itself, (a) to (c) read from the page images and (d) text against data: (a) Table 7.1 gives 306 W against 129 and 131 W, about 2.4 times, while the text says "some three times greater" (PDF pp. 423-424). Inference: Figs 7.10-7.12 show peak power of about 350 against about 125-130 on the plotted scale, nearer three times, so the text may describe the figures rather than the table. (b) Fig 7.10's force curve starts at about 170 and peaks at about 230 near 20-40% of displacement, then declines slowly; the text says peak force is "near the beginning" (PDF p. 424). (c) Fig 7.12's combined force curve rises to about 350 by about 30%, holds, and is highest at about 85-90% before a sharp drop at the end; the double peak "near the beginning and the end of range" in finding 4 is not visible in this printed curve (PDF p. 424). (d) The 7.3 opening says greatest force is "usually ... possible after the joint has passed through the midpoint of the movement" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411), yet the free-weight data here put force highest early. Inference: the opening speaks of maximal joint strength across the range; Fig 7.10 shows force applied to a given accelerating load. Zatsiorsky describes ascending, descending and concave strength curves, with elbow flexion strongest at about 90 degrees ([[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]]), so "after the midpoint" is not a general rule. Velocity and acceleration in Figs 7.10-7.12 share one unlabelled axis with force and power, so their plotted heights cannot be read as m/s.
    31	
    32	**Example** — The study itself: in the combined condition, mean force was 336 N against 184 N under free weight, while peak power was 131 W against 306 W (Table 7.1, PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412, checked against the page image).

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. - Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

155	    14	# Twenty-Two Observations Any Hypertrophy Formula Must Satisfy
156	    15	
157	    16	**What it is** — The authors argue that "Any Hypertrophy Formula has to be based on many well-known observations on muscle physiology and mechanics," and that the target is really "musculo-collagenous hypertrophy, since training affects the entire muscle complex, not just the muscles" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). They list 22 observations (PDF pp. 430-431 / printed pp. 419-420, checked against the page images). Inference: the six groups below are this entry's grouping; the wording inside quotes is theirs.
158	    17	
159	    18	- Stimulus and limit: "The fundamental stimulus in all strength and tissue hypertrophy quite simply is physical loading" (1), which "must not exceed the mechanical strength of the tissues involved" (2); growth can also be stimulated by "active muscle contraction, passive stretching, vibrational oscillation or external electrical stimulation" (22).
160	    19	- Threshold and overload: increase "is minimal unless a certain minimal threshold load is imposed" (5); "The minimal threshold is not fixed, but increases with level of adaptation, which ensures that rate of progress slows down or ceases" (6); continued increase needs "progressive incremental increase in loading" (10).
161	    20	- Timing: gains occur "predominantly during a certain recovery period after loading" (3); they are "not linear or continuous. For example, a 10% increase in load does not necessarily produce a 10% increase in strength" (11); they "diminish if physical loading is not imposed regularly" (21).
162	    21	- Tissue differences: "All tissues do not hypertrophy or strengthen at the same rate or to the same degree" (4); fibre groups differ in fatigue and force (18); "Increase in strength is not necessarily associated with increase in hypertrophy or vice versa" (20).
163	    22	- How tension is made: effects depend on "the way in which the tension is produced or maintained," for example "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load" (8); tension "varies between zero and a certain maximum as joint angles change" (16) and across concentric, eccentric and isometric modes (17).
164	    23	- Nervous system and fatigue: "Muscles rarely are able to produce 100% of their maximum potential" because of protective reflex inhibition (12); gains "may or may not be associated with some form of fatigue" (13); fatigue limits and reflex inhibition are hard to tell apart (14); fatigue is "multi-faceted" (15); and gains "ultimately are the result of specific patterns of nervous excitation" (19).
165	    24	
166	    25	Their conclusion: these "should suffice to show that a 'Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly prescriptive rule is oversimplistic" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).
167	    26	
168	    27	**Why it works** — The list works as a set of constraints: any single-variable rule (one tempo, one rep count, one tension time) will violate several observations at once, such as the rising threshold (6), non-linearity (11) and the different ways tension can be produced (8) (PDF pp. 430-431). The authors cite no studies for the 22 items and call them "well-known observations."
169	    28	
170	    29	**When to apply** — When judging a hypertrophy prescription or a coach's formula, test it against the list: does it overload above a threshold that rises, allow recovery, vary how tension is made, and accept that size and strength can move separately? Eric's baseline: "The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 180, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the band approach fits the authors' view better than a single formula, since it sets ranges rather than one prescriptive number.
171	    30	
172	    31	**When NOT to apply** — The list is uncited. Inference: `supported` rests on several items agreeing with other library sources (the threshold and overload items agree with [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and item 4 with [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]), not on evidence given here. It is a set of constraints, not a prescription: it gives no loads, sets, reps or frequencies. Item 22's passive stretching, vibration and electrical stimulation are listed without doses or comparisons. The section is framed around bodybuilding (bone hypertrophy is "of little consequence to the bodybuilder because bone size and definition are not seen by spectators," PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). Inference: athletes whose priority is performance need more than this list to set loads.
173	    32	
174	    33	**Example** — The authors' item 8 example: tension can be raised either with "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load (in accordance with Newton II: Force = Mass x Acceleration)" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).
175	    34	
176	    35	**Related** — [[claim--time-under-tension-alone-does-not-determine-hypertrophy]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (1.13, the authors' two types of hypertrophy), [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (strength and size as separate training effects)

191	    14	# Time Under Tension Alone Does Not Determine Hypertrophy: Tension Must Exceed a Threshold, and How It Is Produced Matters
192	    15	
193	    16	**What it is** — The authors take on one formula: "every exercise must maintain a prolonged muscle tension time for at least 40 seconds or so if one wishes to produce maximal hypertrophy" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Their counter-claims: "The concept of tension time per se is meaningless, since loading even for very prolonged periods may have no effects of strength and hypertrophy if the tension does not exceed this minimum threshold" (item 7); "The effects of tension on tissue depend not only on the magnitude or duration of the tension, but the way in which the tension is produced or maintained" (item 8); and "Long periods of muscle 'time under tension' as imposed by cyclical activities such as endurance running, cycling and swimming are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy" (item 9) (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420, checked against the page image). They conclude that "a 'Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly prescriptive rule is oversimplistic" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).
194	    17	
195	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the threshold: if tension is below the minimum that triggers adaptation (item 5), adding time does not help (item 7), and endurance sports are their natural experiment of long tension time without growth (item 9) (PDF pp. 430-431). They also note tension can be raised by acceleration as well as mass, "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load" (item 8), so a slow tempo is not the only route to high tension.
196	    19	
197	    20	**When to apply** — When an athlete or coach prescribes slow tempos to hit a fixed tension time, check first that the load is heavy enough to matter (items 5 and 7). Inference: in athletes whose goal is power, do not slow the bar at the cost of intent to reach a tension time. Eric's baseline: "Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 109, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the authors' point supports that stance, since no single number, tension time included, should drive the programme.
198	    21	
199	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The section cites no hypertrophy studies; `supported` rests on the threshold argument and item 9's endurance-sport observation, not on trials comparing tempos. Two voices need separating. The opening quotes are from unnamed commentators, not the authors: "All the big bodybuilders who I trained with did their reps pretty fast, which makes me seriously question the Time Under Tension theory" and "People with extreme genetics who are using huge amounts of drugs will probably get big no matter what kind of weight training and rep speed they're doing. What's more important is finding out how much rep speed matters for a natural bodybuilder with average genetics" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). The authors endorse only the second, saying its author "is probably far closer to the truth than anyone who religiously propounds simplistic Tension Time theories" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420). The closing paragraph on marketing and the public's taste for "cerebrally undemanding mantras" (PDF p. 431) is opinion with no evidence. The claim does not say tension time is irrelevant, only that it is not sufficient on its own.
200	    23	
201	    24	**Example** — The authors' own: endurance running, cycling and swimming impose long "time under tension" but "are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Box Squat With Free Weights Plus Elastic Bands: Greater Force Through the Range and a Faster Descent
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors describe a box squat in a power rack "with strong elastic bands attached between the ends of the bar and the base of the rack," band length set so resistance "varied between set limits at the lowest and the highest positions" (PDF pp. 424-425 / printed pp. 413-414, checked against the page images). The powerlifters (number not given) had "in addition to the squat weight of 200kg, an added elastic resistance of 150kg at the lowest position while sitting down on the box with knees at approximately right angles and a greatest elastic resistance of 250kg at the top of the squat with knees fully extended" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). The stated differences from free-weight training: "1. A greater mean and peak force were produced throughout the range of movement. 2. The descent onto the box tended to be accelerated above the normal gravitational rate of 9.8m/sec squared, so that greater eccentric force had to be generated to control the downward motion. 3. The stronger eccentric loading and the brief transition period involved while sitting before exploding upwards provided neuromuscular stimulation which approximates that usually encountered in popular plyometric training. 4. The force generated during the later stages increased, in strong contrast to the situation of normal squatting in which force production tends to decrease significantly" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). Fig 7.13 (checked against the page image) plots force as a percentage of the bar weight against time: the elastic component runs from about 125% at the top to 75% at the bottom (150/200 and 250/200, matching the text); combined resistance runs from about 225% at the top to about 175% at the bottom and back to about 225%; the eccentric phase spans about 0 to 2.3 s, the box transition about 2.3 to 3.1 s, and the concentric phase about 3.1 to 6 s. The force attributed to the weight itself dips to about 90% during the descent and rises to about 120% early in the ascent.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is items 2 and 3 above: band recoil accelerates the descent beyond gravity, demanding more eccentric force, and the short pause on the box before driving up resembles plyometric loading (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). Item 4 follows from the band tension rising as the lifter stands. The 7.3 opening gives the general reason for variable resistance: force capacity "changes with joint angle," so "any given load will tend to underload certain muscles over some part of the movement range" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — To raise force late in the range of a squat, deadlift, bench or clean where the free-weight load underloads the stronger positions. The authors extend the method to "the deadlift, the clean, the bench press, good mornings and one arm deadlifts," to bands between fixed and moving parts of pulley machines, and to chains, "pioneered in the USA by Louie Simmons primarily for powerlifting purposes," where "as the weight is lifted further off the floor, the more links of chain are raised and the more the resistance increases" (PDF pp. 425-426 / printed pp. 414-415, checked against the page images). Calibration: stand on a bathroom scale holding the bar with stretched cable at the start and end positions, or hang loads from a band to draw "a load vs extension graph" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). For power, the authors cap loads at "about 60-70 percent of one's maximum" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: with bands, the bar's %1RM no longer describes the load at the top or bottom, so a Prilepin prescription needs the band tension stated beside it.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Contested. Frost et al. 2010 (a narrative biomechanical review) state that bands may sustain late-phase force or velocity, but "improved transfer to sport had not been demonstrated and much acute evidence showed no difference from load-matched free weights" (vault brief, review p. 21). That is a named library source against the authors' item 1 and their claim that bands "may be used very effectively" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). In the other direction, Rhea et al. 2009 (48 NCAA Division I men, 12 weeks) found jump power rose 17.8% with fast squats plus bands, 11.0% with fast squats and 4.8% with slow squats; bands beat slow training (p = .02) but not fast-only training (p = .09), and squat strength did not differ (vault brief, pp. 4-5). The authors themselves warn of "large individual variations" and that the curve "depends on the magnitude of the weights load relative to the top and bottom resistance provided by the elastic bands" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). The study is described without sample size or statistics. A faster, band-driven descent raises eccentric force, so the authors' caution on accelerated eccentrics applies ([[framework--four-forms-of-accelerated-powermetrics]]). Inference: this is not in conflict with the 4.2.2 warning that pure elastic resistance "begins from zero" and should not be used for starting or explosive strength ([[framework--inertial-flywheel-and-elastic-band-resistance-devices]]), because here the bands sit on top of a 200 kg bar.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: 200 kg on the bar, bands adding 150 kg on the box and 250 kg at lockout, so the lifter meets about 350 kg at the bottom and about 450 kg at the top (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414; the totals are this entry's arithmetic from the stated values, and match Fig 7.13's 175% and 225%).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[case-study--fradd-free-weight-isokinetic-and-combined-elbow-flexion]], [[framework--four-forms-of-accelerated-powermetrics]], [[framework--inertial-flywheel-and-elastic-band-resistance-devices]], [[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]], [[research-papers/frost-2010-a-biomechanical-evaluation-of-resistance]], [[research-papers/rhea-2009-alterations-in-speed-of-squat-movement-and-the-use-of-accommodated-resistance-among-colleg]], [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]]

    13	
    14	# Four Forms of Accelerated Powermetrics: Raising Force by Acceleration Instead of Added Mass
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The passage is written in the first person by one author ("Let me now elaborate," PDF p. 426 / printed p. 415). Inference: it sits in the Siff and Simmons context of 7.3 (Fig 7.9 and "The author has used ...", PDF p. 422) and is probably Siff's, but the page does not name him. Bands can "accelerate the load during the eccentric phase, thereby providing involuntary or passive acceleration," like plyometrics, where greater force in the amortisation phase comes from "momentum acting on the body through the acceleration of gravity (e.g., during a drop jump) or the action of a propelled object." There is also "an active or voluntary form ... which may be called actively accelerated powermetrics," usable in "the bench press, squat, dip for the jerk, 'Romanian deadlift' (or mid range clean pull from the hang)" and needing no partner or "plyometric bench" (PDF p. 426 / printed p. 415, checked against the page image). The four forms (same page):
    17	
    18	1. Passively accelerated eccentrics with bands: "allow the elastic tension to accelerate the bar during this phase. Then, after a suitable range of movement, halt the movement as rapidly as you can."
    19	2. Passively accelerated eccentrics with a partner, who pushes the bar down "like an inverse form of "forced reps"."
    20	3. Actively accelerated eccentrics: "deliberately pull the bar downwards as fast as you can and stop the downward motion before you reach the end of the movement." Unlike bands, "the force added to gravitational force ceases if one stops voluntarily accelerating the bar."
    21	4. Actively accelerated ballistics (rebounds): pull down as fast as possible, stop "at a suitable point before the end of the movement and as rapidly as you can, try to accelerate the bar upwards into a powerful concentric movement."
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — The stated principle: "this form of training, according to Newton's Second Law, focuses on force being increased by means of acceleration and not added mass" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416, checked against the page image). The author calls it "really a type of 'supramaximal' force training" (same page). No measurements of the forces produced are given.
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — When an athlete needs higher eccentric and amortisation forces than the bar weight alone supplies, without heavier loads or drop equipment. Start "with relatively light loads in the bench press or squat (say, about 40-50kg, depending on your strength and training experience) and use very few repetitions," with "considerably lower" loads for smaller muscle groups (PDF pp. 426-427 / printed pp. 415-416). Load ceiling: "maximal power production, depending on the specific exercise, occurs with loads of between 50-70 percent of one's 1RM, so it is unnecessary ever to exceed this range of loading in these accelerated training methods (unless one uses them over a very small range of motion)" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides)). Inference: these are advanced options for that already-strong group, not for athletes still building relative strength.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — The author warns: "do not overestimate your capabilities, because all of these forms of accelerated powermetrics can be very demanding on the body," and they "can impose extremely large stresses on your soft tissues" (PDF pp. 426-427 / printed pp. 415-416). For safety "do not allow the accelerated load to force you into your extreme end position of joint action" (PDF p. 426). No training study, injury data or force data are given: confidence `untested`. The book gives two power-load ranges six pages apart: "about 60-70 percent of one's maximum" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411) and "between 50-70 percent of one's 1RM" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Both differ from the Chapter 3 figures of about 25% of maximal force in isotonic laboratory models and about two-thirds of maximum in the competition squat ([[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]]); Jandacka and Vaverka 2008 put the acceleration-phase optimum at 47-63% 1RM by sex and exercise in untrained students (vault brief, p. 11). Inference: treat 50-70% as a broad zone, not a fixed number.
    28	
    29	**Example** — The author's own starting point: an accelerated-eccentric bench press or squat with "about 40-50kg" and very few repetitions (PDF p. 426 / printed p. 415). Inference: an actively accelerated ballistic bench at that load would be pulled down fast, stopped a few centimetres above the chest, and driven up at once.
    30	
    31	**Related** — [[case-study--box-squat-with-free-weights-plus-elastic-bands]] (band-accelerated descent), [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]], [[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]], [[research-papers/jandacka-2008-a-regression-model-to-determine-load-for-maximum-power-output]], [[research-papers/handford-2024-a-conceptual-framework-of-different-eccentric-training-methods]] (maps accelerated eccentric loading among eccentric methods), [[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Core Stabilisation on Balls and Boards, and Cueing the Transversus Abdominis, Have No Shown Transfer to Sport
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors write that, "largely as a consequence of individuals attempting to extrapolate to the general fitness world some of the muscle isolating methods used by physical therapists for injury rehabilitation, it has become fairly fashionable to encounter special programmes to train 'core stabilisation' with balancing tools such as wobble boards and physio balls, augmented by activation of the transversus abdominis (TA) to strengthen the trunk." Three objections follow. First, "stability of the core or trunk cannot be exhibited without the periphery of the body being firmly secured on a solid surface, unless, of course, the athlete has to use the core independently of the floor or any other apparatus, as in diving, trampolining and jumping." Second, "Well meaning instructions to activate TA during dynamic actions such as lifting and wrestling are highly inappropriate, because conscious intervention in any such movements can lead to "paralysis by analysis"," and "if the athlete is taught the optimal way to carry out any movement, the body naturally activates muscles in the most appropriate way for that given activity. After all, the body "knows only of movement, not muscles"." Third, "no research has yet shown that isolationist training or ball/board balancing skills transpose to 'functional' sporting action, so that time spent on such pursuits usually can be better spent on more sport specific drills, unless the aim is to resolve some injury." (All PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416, checked against the page image.)
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning rests on two earlier points in the same section: isolation is load-dependent, "Isolation may occur to a significant extent when the resistance to movement is small, but with increasing load, the relevant stabilisers of the body and joints, as well as assistant movers, come more strongly into play," and "all human movement involves the intricate orchestration of concurrent and sequential contractions of movers and stabilisers" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Inference: if stabilisers are recruited by the task and load, a well-learned loaded movement already trains them, and a separate isolation drill adds little; the book states the premises, not this full chain.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When an athlete's programme spends time on unstable-surface or TA-isolation drills, ask whether that time would be better spent on loaded, sport-specific work, and keep coaching cues external to the movement rather than to a single muscle. The exception the authors grant is rehabilitation: "unless the aim is to resolve some injury" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416), which in Baylor terms is Athletic Medicine's call. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — "No research has yet shown" is a statement about the evidence when the book was written, with no citation, and the book gives no study of its own: confidence `untested`. No entry in the vault or staging library covers core stability or unstable-surface training, so the claim could not be checked against another library source. The authors themselves exempt sports where the core works without a fixed base ("diving, trampolining and jumping") and injury rehabilitation. "Paralysis by analysis" is asserted, not measured.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: instructing a lifter or wrestler to brace the transversus abdominis during the action, which they call "highly inappropriate" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Inference: a coach would instead teach the squat or the takedown well and let trunk activation follow the task.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]] (4.2.9, cited by the authors as the earlier discussion), [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]] (the "Limitations of Anatomical Movement Analysis" section 7.4 asks the reader to bear in mind), [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Do Heel Raises With Inversion to Load All Plantarflexors, and Train Dorsiflexion With Both Inversion and Eversion
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors: "so-called 'calf raises' or 'heel raises' are commonly regarded as exercises to develop gastrocnemius and soleus. However, it should be noted that plantarflexion also involves action of plantaris, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior. Moreover, inward rotation or inversion of the foot more strongly recruits the last three muscles named, so that heel raises with inversion tend to activate all of the plantarflexors more strongly." And: "Popular emphasis on heel raising invariably causes one to neglect the antagonistic action of the dorsiflexors such as tibialis anterior. The summary above reveals that it is important to dorsiflex with both inversion and eversion of the ankle if all dorsiflexors are to be exercised adequately." (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418, checked against the page image; the text has a stray "in" in "heel raising in invariably".) The 7.4.1 summary it rests on lists dorsiflexion as "Tibialis anterior, peroneus tertius, extensor hallucis longus, and extensor digitorum longus," inversion as "Flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior, assisted by extensor hallucis longus," and eversion as "Extensor digitorum longus, peroneus tertius, peroneus longus, peroneus brevis" (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The reasoning is the joint-action summary itself: each dorsiflexor also inverts (tibialis anterior) or everts (peroneus tertius, extensor digitorum longus), so one straight dorsiflexion pattern under-loads one side, and the deep plantarflexors that also invert are loaded more when inversion is added (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). No EMG data are given. Inference: confidence `supported` rests on the joint actions being standard functional anatomy, not on any outcome data for the training advice.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Programming calf and shin work for running, jumping and cutting athletes, or when an athlete's lower-leg work is heel raises only. Eric's baseline: "The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 78, Inferred (protocol)). Inference: that test loads plantarflexion in a neutral foot position; the authors' point suggests the training side should also include inverted heel raises and dorsiflexion in both directions, while the test stays standardised.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The two lists do not fully agree, as printed. The 7.4.2 passage names tibialis posterior among the muscles that inversion "more strongly recruits," but the 7.4.1 inversion list does not include tibialis posterior, and the 7.4.1 plantarflexion list does not include flexor hallucis longus, which 7.4.2 names as a plantarflexor (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: check the tibialis posterior omission against an anatomy reference before teaching the 7.4.1 list as complete; the book does not resolve it. This is advice for assistance work; it does not replace the loading of gastrocnemius and soleus that sprinting and jumping demand ([[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]]). Loaded inversion is not a choice for an athlete with an acute lateral ankle sprain without Athletic Medicine's direction.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own example is the heel raise and its neglected antagonist, tibialis anterior (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: a weekly lower-leg block could pair standing heel raises with the foot turned in with banded dorsiflexion done once toward inversion and once toward eversion.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]] (3.7, the graphical form of the same joint-action data), [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]], [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]], [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--isometric-set-positions-ankle-knee-hip]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Trunk Rotation Comes From the Obliques, Not the Erector Spinae, and Trunk Flexion Is Not Rectus Abdominis Alone
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Four trunk claims from 7.4.2 (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418, checked against the page image): (1) the erector spinae "Acting unilaterally ... serve to laterally extend the trunk, whereas acting bilaterally and symmetrically, they extend the trunk backwards without any lateral movement occurring"; (2) "lateral action of the long muscles of the back does not produce spinal rotation and ... the only muscle of the back which is involved in spinal rotation is multifidus. The major initiators of trunk rotation are the internal and external obliques and the strengthening of these muscles, therefore, is vital for all sporting activities that require rotation of the trunk"; (3) rectus abdominis "does not produce any lateral action of the trunk," while "Both groups of obliques acting bilaterally produce trunk flexion so as to augment action by rectus abdominis, so it is incorrect to state that trunk flexion is solely a result of contraction of rectus abdominis"; (4) "if situps are done with a lateral flexing of the trunk, the rectus abdominis are not significantly involved, but the obliques and psoas are strongly contracted." The 7.4.1 summary gives rotation as "The external abdominal obliques of one side acting in conjunction with the opposite internal oblique" and lateral flexion as unilateral iliocostalis and longissimus, both obliques, quadratus lumborum and psoas (PDF p. 428 / printed p. 417, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' basis is the joint-action summary of 7.4.1 and the Movement Matrices of 3.7, which they say let us "appreciate how ill understood some popular exercises are" (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). They give no EMG or cadaver data in this section.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — The authors' own scope is "all sporting activities that require rotation of the trunk" (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: for throwers, batters and linemen who drive and turn, load rotation through the obliques rather than relying on back extensions, and when trunk flexion work is crunches only, add oblique-dominant patterns. Inference: the PNF trunk rotation pattern of Fig 7.8, done supine or standing with cable resistance, is the book's own tool for this (PDF p. 420 / printed p. 409, checked against the page image; see [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]]).
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The claim that multifidus is "the only muscle of the back" involved in spinal rotation is stated without citation. Inference: check this sentence against an anatomy reference before teaching it as exact. Claim (4) is given without data. Before any multi-joint analysis the authors themselves tell the reader to remember the end of Chapter 3: single-joint labels miss that "muscles which do not span other joints can still produce acceleration about those joints" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416; [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]]). Confidence `supported` covers the broad joint-action claims, not the multifidus sentence.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: sit-ups done with a lateral flex shift work from rectus abdominis to the obliques and psoas (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]], [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]], [[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]], [[claim--core-stability-balance-training-has-no-shown-transfer-to-sport]], [[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]] (3.5, trunk actions used for stretching)
######## framework--observations-any-hypertrophy-formula-must-satisfy.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "7.6"
     7	topic: hypertrophy programming constraints
     8	category: [hypertrophy, adaptation, overload, programming]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Twenty-Two Observations Any Hypertrophy Formula Must Satisfy
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors argue that "Any Hypertrophy Formula has to be based on many well-known observations on muscle physiology and mechanics," and that the target is really "musculo-collagenous hypertrophy, since training affects the entire muscle complex, not just the muscles" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). They list 22 observations (PDF pp. 430-431 / printed pp. 419-420, checked against the page images). Inference: the six groups below are this entry's grouping; the wording inside quotes is theirs.
    17	
    18	- Stimulus and limit: "The fundamental stimulus in all strength and tissue hypertrophy quite simply is physical loading" (1), which "must not exceed the mechanical strength of the tissues involved" (2); growth can also be stimulated by "active muscle contraction, passive stretching, vibrational oscillation or external electrical stimulation" (22).
    19	- Threshold and overload: increase "is minimal unless a certain minimal threshold load is imposed" (5); "The minimal threshold is not fixed, but increases with level of adaptation, which ensures that rate of progress slows down or ceases" (6); continued increase needs "progressive incremental increase in loading" (10).
    20	- Timing: gains occur "predominantly during a certain recovery period after loading" (3); they are "not linear or continuous. For example, a 10% increase in load does not necessarily produce a 10% increase in strength" (11); they "diminish if physical loading is not imposed regularly" (21).
    21	- Tissue differences: "All tissues do not hypertrophy or strengthen at the same rate or to the same degree" (4); fibre groups differ in fatigue and force (18); "Increase in strength is not necessarily associated with increase in hypertrophy or vice versa" (20).
    22	- How tension is made: effects depend on "the way in which the tension is produced or maintained," for example "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load" (8); tension "varies between zero and a certain maximum as joint angles change" (16) and across concentric, eccentric and isometric modes (17).
    23	- Nervous system and fatigue: "Muscles rarely are able to produce 100% of their maximum potential" because of protective reflex inhibition (12); gains "may or may not be associated with some form of fatigue" (13); fatigue limits and reflex inhibition are hard to tell apart (14); fatigue is "multi-faceted" (15); and gains "ultimately are the result of specific patterns of nervous excitation" (19).
    24	
    25	Their conclusion: these "should suffice to show that a 'Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly prescriptive rule is oversimplistic" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).
    26	
    27	**Why it works** — The list works as a set of constraints: any single-variable rule (one tempo, one rep count, one tension time) will violate several observations at once, such as the rising threshold (6), non-linearity (11) and the different ways tension can be produced (8) (PDF pp. 430-431). The authors cite no studies for the 22 items and call them "well-known observations."
    28	
    29	**When to apply** — When judging a hypertrophy prescription or a coach's formula, test it against the list: does it overload above a threshold that rises, allow recovery, vary how tension is made, and accept that size and strength can move separately? Eric's baseline: "The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 180, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the band approach fits the authors' view better than a single formula, since it sets ranges rather than one prescriptive number.
    30	
    31	**When NOT to apply** — The list is uncited. Inference: `supported` rests on several items agreeing with other library sources (the threshold and overload items agree with [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and item 4 with [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]), not on evidence given here. It is a set of constraints, not a prescription: it gives no loads, sets, reps or frequencies. Item 22's passive stretching, vibration and electrical stimulation are listed without doses or comparisons. The section is framed around bodybuilding (bone hypertrophy is "of little consequence to the bodybuilder because bone size and definition are not seen by spectators," PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). Inference: athletes whose priority is performance need more than this list to set loads.
    32	
    33	**Example** — The authors' item 8 example: tension can be raised either with "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load (in accordance with Newton II: Force = Mass x Acceleration)" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).
    34	
    35	**Related** — [[claim--time-under-tension-alone-does-not-determine-hypertrophy]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (1.13, the authors' two types of hypertrophy), [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (strength and size as separate training effects)

     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning

     6	chapter: "7.6"
     7	topic: time under tension
     8	category: [hypertrophy, tempo, loading, programming]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Time Under Tension Alone Does Not Determine Hypertrophy: Tension Must Exceed a Threshold, and How It Is Produced Matters
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors take on one formula: "every exercise must maintain a prolonged muscle tension time for at least 40 seconds or so if one wishes to produce maximal hypertrophy" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Their counter-claims: "The concept of tension time per se is meaningless, since loading even for very prolonged periods may have no effects of strength and hypertrophy if the tension does not exceed this minimum threshold" (item 7); "The effects of tension on tissue depend not only on the magnitude or duration of the tension, but the way in which the tension is produced or maintained" (item 8); and "Long periods of muscle 'time under tension' as imposed by cyclical activities such as endurance running, cycling and swimming are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy" (item 9) (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420, checked against the page image). They conclude that "a 'Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly prescriptive rule is oversimplistic" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the threshold: if tension is below the minimum that triggers adaptation (item 5), adding time does not help (item 7), and endurance sports are their natural experiment of long tension time without growth (item 9) (PDF pp. 430-431). They also note tension can be raised by acceleration as well as mass, "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load" (item 8), so a slow tempo is not the only route to high tension.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When an athlete or coach prescribes slow tempos to hit a fixed tension time, check first that the load is heavy enough to matter (items 5 and 7). Inference: in athletes whose goal is power, do not slow the bar at the cost of intent to reach a tension time. Eric's baseline: "Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 109, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the authors' point supports that stance, since no single number, tension time included, should drive the programme.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The section cites no hypertrophy studies; `supported` rests on the threshold argument and item 9's endurance-sport observation, not on trials comparing tempos. Two voices need separating. The opening quotes are from unnamed commentators, not the authors: "All the big bodybuilders who I trained with did their reps pretty fast, which makes me seriously question the Time Under Tension theory" and "People with extreme genetics who are using huge amounts of drugs will probably get big no matter what kind of weight training and rep speed they're doing. What's more important is finding out how much rep speed matters for a natural bodybuilder with average genetics" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). The authors endorse only the second, saying its author "is probably far closer to the truth than anyone who religiously propounds simplistic Tension Time theories" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420). The closing paragraph on marketing and the public's taste for "cerebrally undemanding mantras" (PDF p. 431) is opinion with no evidence. The claim does not say tension time is irrelevant, only that it is not sufficient on its own.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: endurance running, cycling and swimming impose long "time under tension" but "are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).

## FROST
13:tags: ["resistance-training", "ballistic-training", "variable-resistance", "bands", "pneumatic-resistance", "power"]
26:This review provides a mechanical framework for understanding why constant, ballistic, accommodating, and variable resistance produce different force, velocity, power, and muscle-activity profiles.
34:- Narrative review of resistance-training biomechanics rather than a new participant study.
35:- Covers constant free-weight resistance, stretch-shortening-cycle actions, ballistic movements, hydraulic and isokinetic devices, cams and levers, bands and chains, and pneumatic resistance.
36:- The applied context is transfer from gym-based strength and power work to sport performance.
40:- Conceptual and narrative synthesis organized around Newtonian mechanics and published acute studies.
48:- The review concludes that constant resistance creates substantial phase-dependent variation in kinetics and kinematics, while ballistic execution reduces deceleration constraints but does not solve every power-development limitation. [p. 21]
49:- Bands may sustain acceleration and late-phase force or velocity, but the review states that improved transfer to sport had not been demonstrated and much acute evidence showed no difference from load-matched free weights. [p. 21]
50:- Pneumatic resistance has plausible mechanical advantages through lower moving mass, but the hypothesized benefit for sport-specific velocity and power remained untested. [p. 21]
54:- This is a narrative biomechanical review using heterogeneous exercises, devices, populations, loads, and outcome definitions.
56:- Several proposed benefits of bands and pneumatic resistance were theoretical or unsupported by direct transfer studies at publication.
57:- Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): a resistance device cannot be selected from its label alone; exercise, load, intent, range, and athlete status determine the actual stimulus.
61:Start with the adaptation and movement constraint required, then choose a resistance mode that creates the intended force and velocity profile. Ballistic, banded, or pneumatic methods can complement free weights, but the evidence does not justify declaring one mode universally superior; mixed strategies and direct outcome monitoring are more defensible.
67:| Review scope and mechanical framework | pp. 1-2 | review method |
69:| Resistance-mode conclusions and evidence gaps | p. 21 | conclusion |
76:- [[strength-power-transfer]]
## RHEA
12:domain: ["strength-and-conditioning", "power-development"]
22:> Rhea, M. R., Kenn, J. G., & Dermody, B. M. (2009). Alterations in speed of squat movement and the use of accommodated resistance among college athletes training for power. *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 23*(9). https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181b3e1b6
30:Do squat movement speed and accommodating resistance differentially affect jump power and squat strength?
34:- Forty-eight male NCAA Division I baseball, track, football, and basketball athletes.
46:- Jump power improved 17.8% in the fast-plus-bands group, 11.0% with fast squats, and 4.8% with slow squats. [p. 4]
47:- Fast-plus-bands exceeded slow training for power improvement (p = .02); its difference from fast-only did not reach .05 (p = .09). [p. 5]
48:- Squat-strength changes did not differ significantly among groups. [p. 5]
49:- Fast-plus-bands and slow training had similar descriptive strength gains, about 9.4–9.6%. [p. 5]
68:| Between-group tests and strength | p. 5 | result and limitation |
## JAND
11:doi: "10.1080/14763140802266934"
22:> Jandacka, D., & Vaverka, F. (2008). A regression model to determine load for maximum power output. *Sports Biomechanics, 7*(3), 361–371. https://doi.org/10.1080/14763140802266934
34:- Fifty-five male and 48 female physical-education students.
48:- For the acceleration phase, estimated optimal bench-press loads were 56 ± 9% 1RM in men and 63 ± 8% 1RM in women. [p. 11]
49:- Corresponding countermovement-squat loads were 47 ± 9% of maximum dynamic strength in men and 54 ± 9% in women. [p. 11]
50:- Significant sex and exercise effects indicated that a single universal percentage could not represent every task or group. [p. 11]
51:- The authors recommended linking load to the measured force-velocity-power relationship rather than relying only on 1RM percentage. [p. 11]
55:- The sample comprised young physical-education students rather than sport-specific elite athletes.
69:| Exercise- and sex-specific optimal loads | p. 11 | result |
70:| Model-based prescription conclusion | p. 11 | interpretation |

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hh
- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15] Inference: with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes. Ke
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]
- Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4; week1-lecture.md p.9]
- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lectu

**Overall verdict: GO AFTER FIXES.** Of the 14 entries, 4 are GO, 10 need fixes and none is NO-GO. Most of the fixes are small.

I opened every page from PDF 414 to 431 as an image, including 414-418, which the writer had read only as text. Figs 7.10 and 7.12 I zoomed. All the "Eric's baseline:" quotes match their line numbers and tags, and every wikilink points to a file that exists. Neither the voice handling nor the physics and anatomy statements needs a change:
- **7.2 is Siff's:** the page backs this, but Siff is only named on PDF 429 / p.418, and the entries cite PDF 430 alone.
- **Powermetrics passage:** it is correctly marked as an Inference that it's "probably Siff".
- **7.6 commentator quotes:** they are not presented as the authors' own statements.
- **Starling's law, Wolff's law and the multifidus claim:** each is quoted as the book's words, and every comment on them is labelled Inference.
- **Table 7.1 and Fig 7.13:** every value matches the page.
- **60-70% vs 50-70% power-load range:** both figures appear on the cited pages.
- **"Some three times greater":** the gap with the table is real. The table gives about 2.3 to 2.4 times; the plotted figures give about 2.8 to 3.

**Required fixes, one per line:**
1. **All six 7.2 entries:** add PDF 429 / p.418 to the Siff attribution and use the page's wording, "the author ... (Siff, 1989)".
2. **PNF framework:** add principle 4, "Exercising of related muscle groups", which is missing from the grouped list.
3. **Activation/relaxation:** the 7.5 quote is misread. The book's "the latter" means the main exercises, not the stretching. Also, CR and SRHR do come with repetition counts ("a few", "several"), so "without dosages" is wrong.
4. **Fradd:** Fig 7.10 is on PDF 423 / p.412, not 424. Raise `untested` to `supported`, limited to the measured table. Fig 7.12 does show a faint shoulder at about 30%, so soften "double peak not visible". Give the ratio as 2.3 to 2.4.
5. **Box squat:** Frost 2010 and Rhea 2009 are both in the vault and say what the entry claims. But Frost contradicts the book's transfer and "used very effectively" claim, not its item 1, because item 1 compares a heavier total load with plain free weight. Also, the explanation given for item 4 is not in the book, so it needs an "Inference:" label.
6. **Powermetrics:** the Jandacka sample was 55 male and 48 female physical-education students. The vault summary of the paper never says "untrained".
7. **Trunk:** the book contradicts itself and the entry should say so. Its 7.4.1 summary lists only rectus abdominis and psoas for trunk flexion, and only the obliques for rotation. Both disagree with 7.4.2.

**The 7 `untested` ratings:** Fradd is the only one rated too low, since it has measured data. The other six are claims without data (analogy, opinion, illustration or terminology), so `untested` fits them.

**Duplicates:** none found. No existing entry covers core stability or unstable-surface training.

The report also lists 5 ideas no entry covers. These include apparent mistakes in the book's 7.4.1 joint-action tables (posterior deltoid listed for sagittal-plane shoulder flexion, and an elbow-rotation note) and the point that curls work more than the biceps.

- `review_supertraining_ch7b_opus.md`
- page images: `_renders/r7b_p414.png` to `r7b_p431.png`, plus zoomed `r7b_p423_fig710.png` and `r7b_p424_fig712.png`
